# Where the metal bowl would land if it tipped forward toward the customer

## What is actually there

The big stainless mixing bowl is not sitting on an open worktable behind the counter. It is resting in the small chrome cradle/pan of the vintage spring dial scale (the one with the black schnauzer silhouette on its face, marked "25 lb x 1 lb"), and that scale is standing **on the glass top of the pastry display case itself**, at the case's front-left corner — the same glass surface that carries the little wooden "EcoTensil" tasting-spoon box, the wire rack of stacked white plates and the "Whim of the Day" sign further to the right.

Two measurements from the picture matter:

- The scale is perched right at the **front lip** of the case top. The front edge of its chrome base plate is only about 8–10 cm behind the stainless trim rail that finishes the customer-facing edge of the glass top.
- The bowl is far bigger than what it stands on. It is roughly 35–38 cm (14–15 in) across, while the scale's cradle ring is only about 15 cm and its base plate about 20 cm deep. The bowl therefore already overhangs the scale by about 8–10 cm on every side — which means its front rim is already hanging out over, or within a couple of centimetres of, the front edge of the display case. It visibly overhangs the left end of the case as well.

The bowl also appears to be empty (you can see the shop reflected in its interior), so nothing would spill; it is just 1–2 kg of springy stainless steel.

## Where it would land

Because there is essentially **no landing room** on the case top in front of the scale, a forward tip toward the customer would not deposit the bowl on the glass counter top. It would go straight over the edge:

1. It would roll out of the shallow chrome cradle and pitch forward off the front of the scale.
2. Its rim would immediately clear — or more likely clip and scrape — the stainless trim rail along the customer-facing edge of the case top.
3. It would then fall down the front face of the display case, very probably banging against the front glass panel of the case (the one you see the cookies, brownies and tea jars through) on the way.
4. It would hit **the floor on the customer's side of the counter**, right at the foot of the case near its front-left corner — i.e. on the dark patterned area rug / runner and the adjacent wood floor that are visible in the lower-left foreground of the photograph, essentially where a customer would be standing to order.
5. Total drop is roughly 1.4–1.5 m (case top about 1.15–1.2 m off the floor, plus about 35 cm of scale). An empty steel bowl landing from that height would clang loudly, bounce, and then spin and roll a metre or two out across the customer floor area before settling.

## Side effects worth stating

- The most likely collateral damage is to the case: the bowl's rim scraping or striking the stainless top rail and the front glass panel could chip or crack the glass.
- The scale is light and its base is only a few centimetres from the edge. Shoved forward by the departing bowl and suddenly unloaded, it would very likely tip forward too and could follow the bowl off the front of the case.
- If the bowl went slightly right of straight forward rather than dead ahead, it would sweep the little wooden EcoTensil tasting-spoon box off the case top on its way over.
- If it went slightly left, it would clear the left end of the case entirely and land beside it, near the lower stainless side counter that holds the "Black Dog Coffee & Tea" cards, again on the rug.

## Where it would *not* land

- Not on the glass case top itself — the scale is too close to the front edge and the bowl already overhangs it, so the bowl cannot come to rest there.
- Not on the stack of white plates or the "Whim of the Day" sign; those sit well to the right of the scale, out of a straight-forward fall line.
- Not inside the display case — the case is closed glass.
- Not on the back kitchen counter with the coffee urns and microwave; that is behind the bowl, the opposite direction from the customer.
